site.description: Mahdi Sakib Rahman — Business Automation Expert & SAP S/4HANA Automation Specialist. Driving efficiency through intelligent automation.

hero.subtitle: Most people either manage projects or build software. I do both.

paragraphs: I'm a software developer who moved into business automation because I got tired of watching brilliant systems get run by hand. Over 8+ years and 120+ automated processes, I've worked at the intersection of SAP S/4HANA, RPA, and custom integrations — writing the ABAP, APIs, and workflow logic that let finance, order-to-cash, and operations teams stop babysitting manual work and start trusting it to happen on its own. I don't just automate tasks; I re-engineer the systems around them, so what comes out the other end is reliable, auditable, and built to hold up at production scale.
about.quote: "Automation isn't about removing people — it's about removing friction."

projects.subtitle: Each engagement starts with a real problem and ends with a measurable result. Scroll sideways to walk through the case studies.

items.title: Automated Month-End Close
items.problem: A multinational finance team spent 5 business days each month on manual reconciliations, journal postings, and report generation across S/4HANA.
items.solution: Built an ABAP + Fiori automation suite with scheduled jobs, exception-handling workflows, and an RPA layer for non-SAP source data — closing the books with one-click orchestration.

items.title: Intelligent Order Processing
items.problem: Customer orders arrived across email, EDI, and portals — each entered manually into S/4HANA, with a 6% error rate and slow fulfillment.
items.solution: Deployed a UiPath + Power Automate pipeline that classifies, validates, and posts orders into S/4HANA via OData APIs, with a Fiori dashboard for exceptions.

items.title: ZAB ERP (All Modules)
items.problem: The organization ran on a legacy, poorly-documented ERP with limited modules, forcing teams to maintain parallel spreadsheets for functions the system couldn't handle.
items.solution: Led the full-suite ZAB ERP implementation across finance, inventory, sales, and HR modules — from requirements gathering and configuration to data migration and company-wide rollout — over 1 year.

items.title: S/4HANA Migration Data Engine
items.problem: A legacy ERP-to-S/4HANA migration was blocked by years of inconsistent master data and hundreds of manual mapping spreadsheets.
items.solution: Engineered an automated data-cleansing and validation engine using HANA SQL, Python, and API integrations — turning a 9-month manual effort into a repeatable pipeline.

items.title: SAP S/4HANA Implementation (MM)
items.problem: Procurement and inventory were run through manual purchase requisitions, spreadsheet-based stock tracking, and disconnected supplier records, leaving stock visibility and reorder planning unreliable.
items.solution: Led the end-to-end MM rollout — configuring procurement, inventory management, and valuation, migrating material master data, and integrating goods receipt with finance and the warehouse team — going live in 5 months.

items.title: SAP S/4HANA Implementation (SD)
items.problem: Order-to-delivery tracking lived across phone calls, paper delivery notes, and disconnected spreadsheets, leaving sales and logistics teams unable to see order status in real time.
items.solution: Implemented the SD module end-to-end — order management, pricing, credit control, and delivery/billing integration — connecting sales, warehouse, and finance in one workflow within 5 months.

items.title: SAP S/4HANA Implementation (FICO)
items.problem: Financial close relied on manual journal entries and reconciliations across disconnected ledgers, slowing month-end reporting and limiting real-time visibility into cost centers.
items.solution: Rolled out FI/CO — general ledger, accounts payable/receivable, cost center accounting, and asset accounting — with automated postings and integration to MM/SD, completed in 5 months.

items.title: Incident Management System
items.problem: Safety and operational incidents were reported informally by phone or email, with no central log, making it difficult to track resolution status or spot recurring issues.
items.solution: Built a lightweight Incident Management System for logging, assigning, and tracking incidents to resolution, with status visibility for management, shipped in 15 days.

items.title: VMS (Vehicle Management System)
items.problem: The delivery fleet was tracked manually through logbooks and phone check-ins, making it hard to monitor vehicle utilization, maintenance schedules, and trip history.
items.solution: Built a custom Vehicle Management System to log trips, fuel usage, maintenance schedules, and driver assignments in one dashboard, delivered in 2 months.

items.title: SAP S/4HANA Implementation (PM)
items.problem: Equipment maintenance was tracked on paper logs and informal schedules, causing missed preventive maintenance and reactive, costly breakdowns.
items.solution: Implemented the PM module — equipment master data, maintenance planning, work orders, and notifications — enabling scheduled preventive maintenance across facilities in 4 months.

items.title: Rack-Based Inventory Management
items.problem: Warehouse stock was tracked at a general location level without rack-level detail, causing slow picking, misplaced stock, and inaccurate inventory counts.
items.solution: Built a rack-based inventory system that maps stock to specific rack and bin locations, speeding up picking and improving count accuracy, delivered in 1.6 months.

items.title: Sales Force Management
items.problem: Field sales activity — visits, orders, and territory coverage — was reported back to the office manually at the end of each day, with no real-time visibility into the sales team's activity.
items.solution: Developed a Sales Force Management tool for field reps to log visits and orders in real time, giving management live visibility into territory coverage and performance, in 1.5 months.

items.title: Cylinder Tracking System
items.problem: LPG cylinders moved through filling, distribution, and returns with no reliable way to track individual cylinder location, age, or inspection status, risking safety and stock loss.
items.solution: Developed an end-to-end Cylinder Tracking System covering filling, dispatch, distributor handoff, and returns, giving full lifecycle visibility per cylinder, built over 1 year.

items.title: SAP S/4HANA Implementation (Payroll)
items.problem: Payroll processing relied on manual spreadsheets and offline attendance records, creating delays and inconsistencies in salary disbursement and compliance reporting.
items.solution: Implemented SAP Payroll — employee master data, attendance integration, salary structures, and statutory compliance — automating monthly payroll runs within 4 months.

posts.title: Cyber security importance every Sindustry
posts.excerpt: Cybersecurity is no longer just an IT concern. From healthcare and finance to manufacturing, retail, education, and energy, every industry depends on secure digital systems. Learn why cybersecurity is essential for protecting data, maintaining business continuity, building customer trust, and ensuring long-term business resilience.
content: Cybersecurity: A Necessity for Every Industry

In today's digital-first world, almost every business depends on technology. Organizations use cloud platforms, enterprise applications, connected devices, online services, digital payments, and large databases to operate efficiently.
But greater digital dependency also creates greater risk.
Cybercriminals are no longer targeting only technology companies or large financial institutions. Every industry is now a potential target, regardless of its size or business model.
Cybersecurity has therefore become a fundamental part of modern business strategy—not simply an IT responsibility.
Why Cybersecurity Matters Across Industries

Whether it is a hospital protecting patient records, a bank securing financial transactions, or a manufacturing company protecting its production systems, every organization has something valuable to protect.
1. Protecting Sensitive Data
Businesses handle enormous amounts of sensitive information, including:

Customer and employee information
Financial records
Business documents
Intellectual property
Login credentials
Operational data
Supplier and partner information
A successful data breach can expose this information and create serious financial, legal, and reputational consequences.
Strong access controls, encryption, secure authentication, regular backups, and continuous monitoring can significantly reduce these risks.
2. Ensuring Business Continuity
A cyberattack can bring normal business operations to a sudden stop.

Ransomware, for example, can make critical files and systems inaccessible. Attacks against enterprise applications, servers, or operational technology can disrupt everything from customer services to production.
Cybersecurity is therefore closely connected to business continuity and disaster recovery.
Organizations need not only preventive security controls but also tested backup and recovery procedures so that they can continue operating when an incident occurs.
3. Building Customer Trust
Customers expect organizations to protect their information.

A security incident can damage customer confidence even after the technical problem has been resolved. In highly competitive industries, loss of trust can be more damaging than the immediate financial cost of an attack.
Investing in cybersecurity demonstrates that an organization takes privacy, security, and customer protection seriously.
4. Meeting Compliance and Regulatory Requirements
Many industries operate under strict data protection and security requirements.

Financial institutions, healthcare organizations, telecommunications companies, government agencies, and other sectors may have specific regulatory obligations regarding how information is collected, stored, processed, and protected.
A structured cybersecurity program helps organizations identify risks, maintain appropriate controls, and meet applicable compliance requirements.
5. Preventing Financial Loss
Cyberattacks can result in significant financial damage through:

Direct theft or fraud
Operational downtime
Data recovery costs
Legal expenses
Regulatory penalties
Loss of customers
Reputation damage
In many cases, the cost of preventing an incident is considerably lower than recovering from a major security breach.
Cyber Threats Do Not Discriminate
One of the biggest misconceptions about cybersecurity is that only large organizations need serious protection.
In reality, attackers often look for vulnerabilities rather than company size.
A small business with weak passwords, outdated software, poorly configured cloud services, or insufficient employee awareness can be just as vulnerable as a large enterprise.
Common threats include phishing, ransomware, credential theft, malware, social engineering, insider threats, and exploitation of unpatched systems.
Cybersecurity in Different Industries
Cybersecurity has a unique role in every sector.
Healthcare: Protecting patient information and ensuring critical medical systems remain available.
Finance: Securing transactions, accounts, payment systems, and highly sensitive financial information.
Manufacturing: Protecting industrial control systems, production environments, intellectual property, and supply chains.
Retail: Securing customer information, payment systems, e-commerce platforms, and point-of-sale infrastructure.
Education: Protecting student records, research data, learning platforms, and institutional systems.
Energy & Utilities: Securing critical infrastructure and operational technology where disruption can have significant consequences.
Transportation & Logistics: Protecting fleet management systems, tracking platforms, customer information, and operational networks.
Government: Safeguarding public information, critical services, and national infrastructure.
Regardless of the industry, the objective remains the same: protect critical assets and keep essential services running securely.
Building a Strong Cybersecurity Culture
Technology alone cannot solve every cybersecurity problem.
Employees are often the first line of defense. A single compromised password or successful phishing attack can provide attackers with access to otherwise well-protected systems.
Organizations should therefore focus on creating a strong security culture through:

Regular cybersecurity awareness training
Multi-factor authentication
Strong password policies
Least-privilege access
Regular vulnerability assessments
Timely software and security updates
Network segmentation
Secure backups
Incident response planning
Continuous monitoring and logging
Cybersecurity should become part of everyday business operations rather than something considered only after an incident occurs.
The Future of Cybersecurity

As organizations continue adopting cloud computing, artificial intelligence, IoT devices, automation, remote work, and interconnected enterprise systems, the cybersecurity landscape will continue to evolve.
This means organizations must move from a reactive approach to a proactive security mindset.
Regular risk assessments, security monitoring, employee awareness, vulnerability management, and incident response planning can help businesses stay prepared for emerging threats.
Final Thoughts
Cybersecurity is no longer optional or limited to the IT department. It is a business responsibility.
Every organization—regardless of industry, size, or location—depends on digital systems and data. Protecting those assets means protecting the organization itself.
A strong cybersecurity strategy helps businesses protect their data, maintain operations, meet regulatory expectations, preserve customer trust, and build resilience against future threats.
Cybersecurity isn't just about preventing attacks. It's about protecting the future of the business.

posts.title: Software Development Is More Than Coding: Understanding the Business Problem First
posts.excerpt: Great software is not created by writing more code it is created by solving the right problem. Before choosing a technology stack or writing the first line of code, software developers need to understand the business problem, the users, and the outcome the organization actually needs.
content: Introduction
When people hear the term software development, they often think about programming languages, frameworks, databases, APIs, cloud servers, and deployment.
Coding is certainly an important part of software development. But it is only one part of the process.
A technically excellent application can still be a complete failure if it does not solve the right business problem.

Imagine spending six months developing a sophisticated application with a beautiful interface, modern architecture, and hundreds of features—only to discover that employees still use Excel and email because the application does not fit their actual workflow.
This is why successful software development starts before coding.
It starts with understanding the business problem.
1. The Difference Between a Business Problem and a Software Requirement
One of the most common mistakes in software projects is jumping directly from a request to implementation.
For example:
"We need an application to track vehicles."
That is a requirement—but it doesn't explain the actual problem.
A developer should ask:

Why do we need vehicle tracking?
What problem are users currently facing?
How is the process handled today?
Where are delays happening?
Who needs the information?
What decisions will be made using the data?
What does success look like?
Perhaps the real problem is not simply vehicle tracking.

Maybe the organization is losing time because vehicle turnaround information is manually collected, departments cannot see real-time status, and management does not have reliable data for performance analysis.
Now the problem becomes much clearer.
The software is no longer simply a "vehicle tracking application."
It becomes a solution for improving operational visibility, turnaround time, accountability, and decision-making.
That difference matters.
2. Start With "Why?"
Before asking "How will we build it?", ask:
"Why are we building it?"
Understanding the "why" helps developers avoid building unnecessary features.
Consider a simple document approval process.
A business might say:
"We need a document approval portal."
Instead of immediately designing screens and databases, we should understand the existing process.
Perhaps the current workflow looks like:
Employee → Email → Department Head → Manager → Director → Email → Finance → File Storage
This may create several problems:

Approval delays
Lost emails
Lack of visibility
Manual follow-ups
Difficulty tracking approval status
Duplicate documents
No centralized audit trail
The software solution should address those problems—not simply reproduce the same manual process in a digital interface.
3. Understand the Existing Process
Before automating a process, understand how it works today.
This is especially important in business process automation.
A useful approach is to map the existing workflow:
Current Process
Request → Manual Entry → Email → Approval → Data Entry → Reporting
Then identify:

Where does the process start?
Who performs each step?
What information is required?
Where is information stored?
Which steps are manual?
Where do errors occur?
Where do users wait?
Which approvals are required?
What happens when something is rejected?
What reports are required?
Once the current process is understood, developers can identify opportunities for improvement.
4. Talk to the People Who Actually Use the System
Business requirements documents are useful, but they don't always tell the complete story.
The people using the process every day often know things that are missing from formal requirements.
For example, management may say:
"Users should submit the request through the system."
But the actual users might explain:
"Sometimes the request is submitted from the factory floor where the internet connection is unstable."
That single piece of information can significantly change the solution.
User discussions can reveal:

Real-world constraints
Hidden manual processes
Exceptions
Workarounds
Common errors
User frustrations
Security concerns
Reporting requirements
Good software development therefore requires communication skills, not just technical skills.
5. Don't Automate a Bad Process
One of the most important principles in business automation is:
Don't automate a broken process without understanding why it is broken.
Suppose an organization requires employees to enter the same information into three different systems.
A developer could automate those three data-entry steps.
But perhaps the better solution is to integrate the systems so the information only needs to be entered once.
Automation should not simply make a bad process faster.
It should make the process better.
A good developer therefore asks:
"Do we really need this step?"
rather than simply asking:
"How can I automate this step?"
6. Technology Should Follow the Problem
Another common mistake is choosing technology before understanding the requirements.
For example:
"Let's build this using React."
or
"Let's use microservices."
or
"Let's move everything to the cloud."
These might be excellent technical choices—but they should not be the starting point.
The better approach is:
Business Problem → Requirements → Process → Architecture → Technology → Development
Technology should serve the business objective.
Sometimes the best solution may be a custom web application.
Sometimes it may be a mobile application.
Sometimes a low-code platform may be enough.
Sometimes the best solution is an API integration between existing systems.
And sometimes the correct answer is:
We don't need new software. We need to improve the existing process.
That's also a successful technology decision.
7. Think About Business Value
Software projects should ultimately create measurable value.
That value might be:

Reducing operational costs
Saving employee time
Reducing manual errors
Increasing productivity
Improving customer experience
Improving compliance
Increasing visibility
Improving decision-making
Reducing processing time
For example, instead of saying:
"We developed a workflow application."
A stronger business outcome would be:
"The new workflow reduced manual approval follow-ups and provided real-time visibility into pending requests."
The second statement explains why the software matters.
8. Developers Should Understand the Business Domain
A developer doesn't necessarily need to become a business expert.
But understanding the business domain can dramatically improve software quality.
For example, an ERP developer working with manufacturing should understand concepts such as:

Procurement
Inventory
Production
Sales
Maintenance
Finance
Supply chain
Warehouse operations
Similarly, someone developing banking software should understand basic banking processes.
Someone building HR software should understand recruitment, payroll, leave, attendance, and employee lifecycle processes.
The more developers understand the domain, the better questions they can ask.
And better questions usually lead to better software.
9. Build Solutions, Not Features
A major difference exists between building features and solving problems.
A feature-oriented approach might look like:

Login
Dashboard
Reports
Notifications
Search
Export
User management
But a problem-oriented approach asks:
"What does the user need to accomplish?"
For example:
Problem: Managers cannot quickly identify delayed operations.
Solution: Provide a dashboard showing real-time operational status, delays, responsible departments, and historical performance.
Now the dashboard is not just a feature.
It is a decision-making tool.
This mindset changes how software is designed.
10. Measure Success After Deployment
Software development doesn't end when the application goes live.
After deployment, ask:

Are users actually using it?
Is the process faster?
Are errors reduced?
Are users satisfied?
Are employees still maintaining parallel Excel files?
Are people bypassing the system?
Are managers receiving better information?
Did the application actually solve the original problem?
Sometimes the answer will be:
"Not completely."
That's valuable information.
Software should continuously evolve based on real-world usage.
11. The Best Developers Ask Better Questions
Technical skills are important.
But great software engineers also know how to ask questions such as:
What problem are we solving?
Who has this problem?
Why does this problem exist?
How is it currently handled?
What happens if we do nothing?
What information is required?
What are the exceptions?
What does success look like?
Can this process be simplified before we automate it?
Is custom software actually necessary?
These questions can prevent weeks or months of unnecessary development.
Conclusion
Software development is not simply about converting requirements into code.
It is about understanding a problem, designing an appropriate solution, implementing it effectively, and creating measurable value for the people and organization using it.
Coding builds the software. Understanding the business builds the right software.
The strongest developers therefore don't start their work with:
"Which programming language should I use?"
They start with:
"What problem are we trying to solve?"
Once that question has a clear answer, technology becomes much easier to choose.
And that is where real software engineering begins.

posts.title: Mail Spoofing & Cyber Security: How to Protect Your Organization from Email-Based Attacks
posts.excerpt: Mail spoofing is one of the most common email-based cyber threats facing organizations today. Learn how attackers impersonate trusted senders, the risks involved, and practical security measures such as SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MFA, and employee awareness that can help keep your organization safe.
content: Email has become one of the most important communication tools for modern organizations. Employees use email every day to communicate with colleagues, customers, vendors, financial institutions, and business partners.
However, email is also one of the most common entry points for cyber attacks.
One particularly dangerous technique is mail spoofing, where attackers manipulate the identity of an email sender to make a message appear as if it came from a trusted person or organization.
A single convincing email can potentially lead to financial loss, data theft, credential compromise, malware infection, or serious reputational damage.
The good news is that organizations can significantly reduce these risks by combining the right technology, security policies, and employee awareness.
What Is Mail Spoofing?
Mail spoofing is a technique where an attacker makes an email appear to come from a trusted sender when it actually comes from an unauthorized source.
For example, imagine that an organization's Finance Department normally uses an address such as:
finance@company.com
An attacker may attempt to send a fraudulent email that appears to be associated with that trusted identity.
The message might say:
“Please process the payment immediately. The bank account details have been updated.”
If an employee trusts the email without verifying the request, the organization could lose money or expose sensitive information.
It is important to understand that email spoofing and account compromise are not exactly the same thing.

With spoofing, an attacker may impersonate a sender without having access to the legitimate mailbox. With account compromise, the attacker may actually gain unauthorized access to a real account and use it to send or receive messages.
Both situations can be dangerous.
Why Is Mail Spoofing Dangerous?
Cyber attacks are not always based on sophisticated technical vulnerabilities. Many attacks target something much simpler: human trust.
Attackers may impersonate:

CEOs and senior executives
Finance officers
HR managers
IT administrators
Customers
Vendors and suppliers
Banks or financial institutions
Government or service providers
A fraudulent email may request:

An urgent payment
A password reset
Sensitive documents
Customer information
Employee information
Bank account changes
Access to an online service
Clicking a suspicious link
Opening an unexpected attachment
The attacker often creates a sense of urgency so that the recipient acts before thinking.
This is why cybersecurity is not only a technical issue. Human awareness is a critical part of organizational security.
A Simple Example of a Spoofing Attack
Imagine an employee receives an email that appears to come from the company's Managing Director.
The email says:
“I am currently in a meeting. Please transfer the payment to the new supplier account today. This is confidential.”
The request may look legitimate.
But there are several warning signs:
1. The request is unusually urgent.
2. The sender is asking for a financial transaction.
3. The employee is told not to verify the request.
4. Bank details may have suddenly changed.
5. The attacker is using the authority of a senior executive to influence the employee.
This type of social engineering is commonly associated with Business Email Compromise (BEC) and executive impersonation scams.
How Does a Mail Spoofing Attack Work?
A typical attack may follow several stages.
1. Information Gathering
Attackers may collect publicly available information about an organization and its employees.
They may look at company websites, social media profiles, public documents, job advertisements, and other sources to understand the organization's structure.
2. Choosing a Target
The attacker may target people who have access to money, confidential information, customer data, or important systems.
3. Creating a Deceptive Identity
The attacker attempts to make the communication appear to come from a trusted individual or organization.
4. Sending the Fraudulent Message
The attacker sends an email containing a request, link, attachment, or other action.
5. Creating Urgency
The attacker may use phrases such as:

“Urgent”
“Immediate action required”
“Confidential”
“Please do this today”
“Do not call me”
“I am unavailable right now”
The goal is to prevent the recipient from carefully verifying the request.
6. Waiting for the Victim to Act
The final step depends on the attacker's objective.
The victim may:

Transfer money
Share information
Click a malicious link
Enter credentials
Open an attachment
Approve an unauthorized request
How Can Organizations Prevent Mail Spoofing?
There is no single security tool that can eliminate every email-based threat.
Organizations should use a layered security approach that combines technology, processes, and employee awareness.
1. Implement SPF
SPF stands for Sender Policy Framework.
SPF allows a domain owner to specify which mail servers are authorized to send email on behalf of that domain.
For example, an organization can publish an SPF record in DNS that identifies its legitimate email-sending services.
SPF can help receiving mail systems detect unauthorized sending sources.
However, SPF should not be treated as a complete solution by itself.
It should be implemented together with DKIM and DMARC.
2. Implement DKIM
DKIM stands for DomainKeys Identified Mail.
DKIM adds a digital signature to outgoing email.
The receiving mail server can verify that signature and determine whether the message passed the relevant domain-level authentication checks and whether signed content was altered in transit.
Proper DKIM configuration strengthens email authenticity and helps protect an organization's domain from abuse.
3. Implement DMARC
DMARC stands for Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance.
DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM and allows organizations to publish a policy describing how receiving mail systems should handle messages that fail authentication.
Common DMARC policies include:

p=none — Monitor and collect information
p=quarantine — Treat suspicious messages as potentially fraudulent
p=reject — Reject messages that fail the required authentication policy
Organizations should normally monitor their legitimate email sources before moving to a strict enforcement policy.
A practical approach is:
Monitor → Analyze → Fix → Enforce
4. Monitor DMARC Reports
Configuring DMARC is only the beginning.
Organizations should regularly review DMARC reports to understand:

Which systems are sending email using their domain
Whether legitimate email services are properly authenticated
Whether unauthorized sources are attempting to use the domain
Whether configuration problems exist
Regular monitoring can help security teams identify suspicious activity early.
5. Enable Multi-Factor Authentication
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) provides an additional layer of protection beyond passwords.
Even if an employee's password is compromised, MFA can make unauthorized access significantly more difficult.
MFA should be enabled for important systems such as:

Corporate email
Cloud platforms
VPN
Administrative accounts
Financial systems
Remote access systems
Privileged accounts
Where available, organizations should consider stronger phishing-resistant authentication methods.
6. Establish a Payment Verification Process
One of the most effective defenses against business email fraud is a clear internal process.
Never rely on email alone for high-value financial transactions.
For example:
New bank account → Independent verification
Bank detail change → Verify through a trusted channel
Large payment → Secondary approval
Executive payment request → Confirm independently
A simple phone call or separate communication channel can prevent a major financial loss.
7. Be Careful With Urgent Emails
Urgency is one of the most common psychological techniques used by attackers.
If an email says:
“Do this immediately.”
“This is confidential.”
“Do not contact anyone.”
“I need this completed within the next 10 minutes.”
Take a moment before responding.
Remember:
Urgency is not proof of authenticity.
A legitimate request can still be verified.
8. Train Employees Regularly
Employees are one of the most important parts of an organization's cybersecurity defense.
Security awareness training should teach employees how to recognize:

Suspicious sender addresses
Look-alike domains
Unexpected attachments
Suspicious links
Fake login pages
Unusual payment requests
Password requests
Unexpected account changes
Social engineering attempts
Training should not be limited to the IT department.
Everyone who uses email is part of the organization's security team.
9. Create an Easy Phishing Reporting System
Employees should have a simple way to report suspicious emails.
For example, organizations can provide a:
“Report Phishing” button
or a dedicated security reporting address.
Most importantly, employees should feel comfortable reporting mistakes.
If someone accidentally clicks a suspicious link, the best response is not to hide the incident.
The best response is:
Report it immediately.
Early reporting can give the security team valuable time to investigate and contain a potential incident.
10. Protect Accounts With Strong Authentication
Organizations should avoid relying only on passwords.
A strong identity security strategy can include:

Unique passwords
Password managers
MFA
Account monitoring
Privileged access controls
Regular access reviews
Immediate access removal when an employee leaves
Employees should never share passwords through email, messaging applications, or phone calls.
11. Use Email Security Solutions
Organizations can deploy email security solutions that analyze incoming messages for suspicious characteristics.
Security systems may evaluate:

Sender reputation
Domain reputation
Authentication results
Suspicious URLs
Attachments
Impersonation indicators
Abnormal communication patterns
These technologies can reduce risk, but they should complement—not replace—employee awareness.
12. Watch for Look-Alike Domains
Attackers may register domains that look similar to legitimate business domains.
For example, an attacker might create a domain with a slightly different spelling or domain extension.
Employees should carefully check the actual sender address instead of relying only on the display name.
Seeing:
“CEO — Company Name”
does not necessarily mean the email came from the real CEO.
Always verify the actual email address and domain.
13. Follow the Principle of Least Privilege
Employees should only have access to the systems and information they actually need.
For example, someone who does not perform financial operations should not automatically have access to financial approval systems.
Organizations should regularly review:

User permissions
Administrator accounts
Financial access
Cloud access
Shared accounts
Former employee accounts
Reducing unnecessary access can limit the impact of a compromised account.
14. Keep Reliable Backups
Cybersecurity is broader than email protection.
Organizations should maintain reliable backups of critical information and systems.
A good backup strategy should include:

Regular backups
Appropriate access controls
Protected or immutable backup copies where appropriate
Monitoring
Restore testing
A backup is only useful if the organization can actually restore its data when needed.
15. Build an Incident Response Plan
No organization should assume that it will never experience a cyber incident.
Instead, organizations should prepare for the possibility.
An incident response plan should clearly define:

Who should be contacted
How suspicious emails should be reported
Who investigates incidents
How compromised accounts are secured
How affected systems are isolated
How customers or partners are notified when necessary
How the organization recovers
Preparation can significantly reduce confusion during a real incident.
The “STOP → CHECK → VERIFY → ACT” Rule
One of the easiest security habits employees can adopt is:
STOP
Do not immediately respond to an unusual request.
CHECK
Check the sender address, domain, link, attachment, and context.
VERIFY
Confirm important requests through an independent and trusted communication channel.
ACT
Only proceed after you are confident that the request is legitimate.
This simple habit can prevent many successful social engineering attacks.
Cybersecurity Is Everyone's Responsibility
Cybersecurity is often viewed as an IT department responsibility.
That mindset needs to change.
The IT and security teams provide the technology and security controls, but employees make decisions every day that can affect the organization's security.
A finance employee verifying a payment request can prevent financial fraud.
An HR employee recognizing a phishing email can prevent credential theft.
A student or intern reporting a suspicious message can help protect the organization.
A manager confirming an unusual request can stop an impersonation attack.
Security is a shared responsibility.
Final Thoughts
Mail spoofing may appear simple, but its consequences can be serious.
Attackers do not always need advanced hacking techniques. Sometimes, all they need is a convincing email and a moment of human error.
Organizations can significantly reduce the risk by combining:
SPF + DKIM + DMARC + MFA + Email Security + Employee Awareness + Payment Verification + Access Control + Monitoring + Incident Response
But technology alone is not enough.
The strongest security strategy is one where technology protects the organization, policies guide employees, and people understand when something does not look right.
So before clicking, replying, sharing information, or approving a payment, remember:

STOP → CHECK → VERIFY → ACT
Stay alert. Stay secure.
Cybersecurity is not just an IT responsibility. It is everyone's responsibility.

posts.title: An Efficient Approach to Detect Melanoma Skin Cancer Using a Custom CNN Model
posts.excerpt: An exploration of using a custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model to detect melanoma skin cancer from skin-lesion images, highlighting the potential of AI as a supportive diagnostic approach.
content: An Efficient Approach to Detect Melanoma Skin Cancer Using a Custom CNN Model
## Introduction

Melanoma is one of the most serious forms of skin cancer. When detected at an early stage, treatment can be significantly more effective. However, identifying melanoma from other types of skin lesions can be challenging because many lesions may have similar visual characteristics.

With the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Deep Learning, computer-based systems are increasingly being explored for medical image analysis. One of the most effective deep learning techniques for image classification is the **Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)**.

In this research, we explored the development of a **custom CNN model for melanoma skin cancer detection**. The goal was to investigate how a deep learning model can analyze skin-lesion images and identify patterns that may indicate melanoma.
> **Important:** The proposed system is designed as a supportive diagnostic approach and is not intended to replace medical professionals or clinical diagnosis.
## Why Melanoma Detection Matters

Melanoma develops from melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing melanin in the skin. Although melanoma is less common than some other types of skin cancer, it can be considerably more dangerous because of its ability to spread to other parts of the body.
Early detection is therefore extremely important.

Traditionally, dermatologists examine suspicious lesions based on their visual characteristics and may recommend additional tests when necessary. However, the increasing availability of digital skin images creates an opportunity to use AI to assist with this process.
An AI-based system could potentially provide an additional layer of analysis and help identify lesions that require closer professional examination.
## The Role of AI in Skin Cancer Detection
Deep learning models are particularly effective at analyzing images because they can automatically learn visual patterns from large collections of training data.
Unlike traditional image-processing approaches where features need to be manually defined, CNNs can learn features directly from images.
For example, a CNN may learn to recognize:

* Shapes and structures of skin lesions
* Differences in color and pigmentation
* Texture patterns
* Irregular borders
* Asymmetry
* Other visual characteristics associated with different lesion classes
These learned patterns can then be used to classify previously unseen images.
## Our Approach
The main idea behind this research was to develop a **custom Convolutional Neural Network** capable of classifying skin-lesion images.
The overall workflow can be represented as:
**Skin Image → Preprocessing → CNN Feature Extraction → Classification → Prediction**
Each stage plays an important role in the final performance of the system.
## 1. Dataset Preparation
The first step was preparing a dataset containing labeled skin-lesion images.
The images were organized according to their respective classes so that the CNN could learn the visual differences between melanoma and other skin lesions.
A well-prepared dataset is essential because the quality and diversity of training data can have a significant impact on the performance of a machine learning model.
The dataset was divided into separate subsets for:

* **Training**
* **Validation**
* **Testing**
This separation helps evaluate whether the model can generalize beyond the images it has seen during training.
## 2. Image Preprocessing
Raw images cannot always be directly provided to a neural network. Therefore, preprocessing was performed before training the model.
The preprocessing pipeline included techniques such as image resizing and pixel-value normalization.
Data augmentation can also be applied to introduce additional variations into the training data. Techniques such as:

* Rotation
* Horizontal or vertical flipping
* Scaling
* Cropping
* Slight image transformations
can help the model become more robust and reduce the risk of overfitting.
## 3. Building the Custom CNN
The core component of the proposed system is the **Custom Convolutional Neural Network**.
CNNs process images through multiple layers. The early layers generally learn simple visual patterns, while deeper layers can learn more complex structures.
A typical architecture consists of:
**Input Image → Convolutional Layers → Pooling Layers → Feature Extraction → Fully Connected Layers → Classification**
### Convolutional Layers
Convolutional layers are responsible for extracting visual features from the image.
At the beginning of the network, these layers may detect simple patterns such as edges and shapes. As the image passes through deeper layers, the network can learn increasingly complex patterns.
### Pooling Layers
Pooling reduces the spatial dimensions of the extracted feature maps while retaining important information.
This helps reduce computational complexity and allows the model to focus on the most important features.
### Fully Connected Layers
After feature extraction, the learned information is passed to fully connected layers.
These layers combine the extracted features and prepare them for the final classification decision.
### Output Layer
The final layer produces the classification result, indicating which category the input image most closely matches.
## 4. Training the Model
Once the architecture and dataset were prepared, the CNN model was trained using the training images.
During training, the model continuously compares its predictions with the actual labels. Based on the prediction error, the network adjusts its internal parameters.
This process is repeated over multiple training cycles, commonly known as **epochs**.
The validation dataset is used during training to monitor whether the model is learning useful patterns or simply memorizing the training images.
## 5. Evaluating Performance
For a medical image classification system, accuracy alone may not provide a complete picture of model performance.
Several metrics can be considered:
### Accuracy
Accuracy represents the overall percentage of correctly classified images.
### Precision
Precision measures how many of the images predicted as positive cases were actually positive.
### Recall
Recall, also known as sensitivity, measures how effectively the model identifies actual positive cases.
For melanoma detection, recall is particularly important because missing a potentially malignant lesion can have serious consequences.
### F1-Score
The F1-score combines precision and recall into a single metric and can be useful when evaluating classification performance.
### Confusion Matrix
A confusion matrix provides a more detailed view of the model's predictions by showing correct and incorrect classifications for each class.
## What Makes This Approach Interesting?
One of the main focuses of this research is the use of a **custom CNN architecture** rather than relying entirely on a pre-trained model.
Developing a custom architecture provides an opportunity to experiment with:

* Network depth
* Number of filters
* Kernel sizes
* Pooling strategies
* Activation functions
* Regularization
* Training parameters
This allows the architecture to be adjusted according to the characteristics of the dataset and the specific classification problem.
## Challenges
Developing an AI system for melanoma detection comes with several challenges.
### Dataset Quality

The model's performance heavily depends on the quality and diversity of the dataset. A model trained on limited or biased data may not perform equally well on images from different populations or environments.
### Class Imbalance

Medical datasets may contain significantly different numbers of samples across classes. If this imbalance is not handled properly, the model may become biased toward the more frequently represented class.
### Overfitting

A CNN can sometimes perform extremely well on training data but poorly on previously unseen images. Techniques such as data augmentation, regularization, and validation monitoring can help address this problem.
### Interpretability
Deep learning models are often considered difficult to interpret. Understanding why the model classified a particular lesion as suspicious is important, especially in medical applications.
## AI as a Supportive Diagnostic Tool
The most important aspect of this research is understanding the role of AI in healthcare.
The purpose of a melanoma detection model should **not** be to replace dermatologists or other qualified healthcare professionals.
Instead, such a system can potentially work as a **supportive diagnostic tool**.

For example, an AI system could analyze an image and indicate that a lesion appears suspicious. A healthcare professional could then use that information alongside clinical examination, patient history, and other appropriate diagnostic procedures.
This human-AI collaboration could potentially make screening processes more efficient while keeping final medical decisions under professional supervision.
## Future Improvements
There are several opportunities for improving the proposed approach in future research.
Potential improvements include:

* Training with larger and more diverse datasets
* Comparing the custom CNN with transfer-learning models
* Using explainable AI techniques
* Improving model robustness across different image sources
* Addressing class imbalance more effectively
* Performing extensive cross-validation
* Testing the model on independent datasets
* Exploring real-time or mobile-based screening applications
Explainable AI is particularly interesting because it could help visualize which parts of a lesion influenced the model's prediction.
## Conclusion
The use of Artificial Intelligence in medical image analysis is opening new possibilities for supporting healthcare professionals.

In this research, we explored an efficient approach for melanoma skin cancer detection using a **custom Convolutional Neural Network model**. The system uses image preprocessing, CNN-based feature extraction, and classification to identify patterns within skin-lesion images.

The research demonstrates the potential of deep learning for assisting with melanoma detection. However, the performance of an AI model should always be interpreted within the limitations of its dataset, training process, and testing environment.
Most importantly, AI should be considered a **supportive technology rather than a replacement for medical expertise**.

With larger datasets, better model architectures, explainable AI, and rigorous clinical validation, AI-assisted skin-lesion analysis could become an increasingly valuable tool for supporting early detection and clinical decision-making.
